chapters.title: Chapter 2: Ensemble Methods I: Bagging and Boosting

lessons.title: Decision Trees to Random Forests: Bagging for Robust Trading Signals

body.text: A single decision tree given enough depth will happily report 90%+ training accuracy on data where the real signal-to-noise ratio, from this course's first chapter, barely clears 52 to 55%. Bagging's entire value proposition is variance reduction, and variance reduction is exactly the medicine a low-signal, high-noise problem like next-day price prediction needs.

children.text: Why a Single Decision Tree Is a Bad Idea on Market Data

A decision tree grows by repeatedly splitting the training data to minimize impurity, and left unconstrained, it will keep splitting until every leaf is small enough to be nearly pure. On rich, stable data like images that is a feature. On data where the real relationship between features and triple-barrier labels is thin and shifts over time, that same greedy splitting behavior is a liability: a deep tree will carve out leaves that fit the specific noise in your training window rather than any structure that survives into the next quarter.

body.text: Low signal-to-noise ratio plus a high-variance model is a guaranteed recipe for overfitting. A single unconstrained decision tree is about the highest-variance model you can build on tabular data, which makes it close to the worst possible starting point for market data on its own, and the best possible illustration of why this chapter exists.

markDefs.definition: Bootstrap aggregating: training many copies of a model, each on a different bootstrap resample (sampling with replacement) of the training rows, then averaging their predictions, for regression, or taking a majority vote, for classification.

children.text: , trains B separate trees, each on its own bootstrap resample of the training rows, then averages their outputs. If each tree's errors were completely independent of the others, averaging B of them would shrink the ensemble's variance by a factor of B. In practice trees trained on overlapping bootstrap samples of the same dataset are correlated with each other, so the real benefit is smaller than that ideal, but still substantial, and it costs you almost nothing in bias, since averaging does not systematically push predictions in any particular direction.

body.caption: σ² is the variance of a single tree, ρ is the average pairwise correlation between trees, and B is the number of trees. As B grows, the second term shrinks toward zero, but the first term, ρσ², does not depend on B at all. Correlation between trees, not tree count, sets the floor on how much bagging can help.

children.text: Random Forest's Extra Trick: Decorrelating the Trees

A random forest is bagging plus one more idea: at every split, each tree is only allowed to consider a random subset of features, not all of them. This pushes ρ, the correlation term in the formula above, down further than bootstrap resampling alone can manage, since two trees are now less likely to keep finding the same dominant split on the same one or two features. Lowering ρ lowers the variance floor the ensemble can never average its way below, which is the entire reason random forests generally outperform plain bagged trees.

body.caption: Random forest hyperparameters, read through a trading lens

cells: Number of trees in the ensemble
More trees mainly reduce the variance of the ensemble's own estimate; returns diminish well before four figures
How many splits a single tree can make
Keep shallow (roughly 3 to 6) given how thin the real signal is; deep trees overfit noise fast on market data
Minimum rows required in a leaf
Set generously; tiny leaves on thin signal are almost always fitting noise, not a genuine pattern
Feature subset size considered per split
Lower values decorrelate trees further (the ρ term above), at some cost to each individual tree's quality

body.code:
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

rf = RandomForestClassifier(
    n_estimators=500,
    max_depth=5,
    min_samples_leaf=50,   # avoid tiny, noisy leaves on thin signal
    max_features="sqrt",   # decorrelate trees further than bootstrapping alone
    oob_score=True,
    random_state=42,
    n_jobs=-1,
)
rf.fit(X_train, y_train)
print(rf.oob_score_)
body.caption: min_samples_leaf=50 and max_depth=5 are doing the real overfitting-control work here. Defaults tuned for dense, high-signal tabular data are almost always too permissive for triple-barrier-labeled market data.

children.text: Out-of-Bag Error: A Free Validation Estimate, With a Catch

Because each tree only trains on a bootstrap resample, a chunk of the training rows never gets seen by any given tree. Averaging each row's predictions across only the trees that never trained on it gives an out-of-bag, or OOB, error estimate, a form of built-in validation that costs nothing extra to compute.

body.caption: The probability a specific row is never selected across n draws, sampled with replacement from n rows, converges to 1/e. In practice, roughly 36.8% of rows are left out of any single tree's bootstrap sample, chosen differently for every tree.

body.label: Out-of-Bag Sample Size
body.context: Each tree naturally never sees a bit over a third of the training rows, a different third for every tree, which is what makes OOB error possible without setting aside a dedicated holdout set.

body.text: OOB error assumes a left-out row is an informative, independent test of a tree's generalization. With triple-barrier labels, holding-period windows for different rows can overlap in time, so a row left out of one tree's bootstrap sample can still be highly correlated with rows that WERE used to train it, an echo of the same leakage risk a shuffled K-Fold split carries. Treat OOB error as a convenient sanity check, never a replacement for the walk-forward validation this course relies on.

children.text: Applying This to a Trading Signal

Take a single unconstrained decision tree and a 500-tree random forest, both trained on the same triple-barrier-labeled Nifty 200 dataset from Chapter 1, and evaluated with proper walk-forward validation, out-of-sample data the model never touched during training. The pattern is almost always the same shape: the single tree posts a very high in-sample accuracy and a walk-forward accuracy barely above chance, while the forest gives up some of that inflated in-sample number in exchange for a walk-forward result that is only modestly better than chance, but genuinely closer to real.

body.text: These figures are an illustrative example built to show the shape of the effect, not results from a specific dataset or model run in this course. Chapter 2's closing case study reports actual walk-forward results for a concrete Nifty 200 momentum signal.

children.text: Bagging builds every tree independently and averages them afterward. The next lesson covers gradient boosting, XGBoost and LightGBM, which builds trees sequentially, each one correcting the mistakes of the ensemble so far, a fundamentally different way to combine trees with its own, sharper overfitting risks on data this thin.

body.title: The Variance Floor From Correlated Trees
body.prompt: Individual trees in your bagged ensemble have a variance of 100 and an average pairwise correlation of 0.25. As the number of trees grows very large, what value does the ensemble's variance approach?
body.explanation: As B grows large, Var(average) approaches ρσ² = 0.25 × 100 = 25. No matter how many trees you add beyond that point, correlation between trees sets a floor the ensemble cannot average its way below, which is exactly why random forest's extra decorrelation trick, restricting each split to a random feature subset, matters more than simply adding more trees.

body.title: Trusting an Out-of-Bag Score
body.question: A random forest trained on triple-barrier-labeled Nifty 200 data reports a strong out-of-bag (OOB) accuracy. Why might this still overstate how the model performs live, even though OOB rows were never used to train the trees that score them?
options: OOB error is a completely unbiased estimate and cannot be overstated

Overlapping triple-barrier event windows mean a row left out of bag for one tree can still be highly correlated with rows that were used to train it, echoing the same leakage risk as a shuffled K-Fold split
OOB error only works for regression problems, not classification
Random forests do not actually support OOB scoring
body.explanation: OOB scoring assumes left-out rows are informative, independent tests of a tree's generalization. When triple-barrier labels come from overlapping holding-period windows, an OOB row can share most of its event window with a row that was used to train the tree, so the 'held-out' test is less independent than it looks. It is the same underlying risk as the shuffled K-Fold problem from Chapter 1, showing up inside a convenience metric instead of an explicit cross-validation loop, which is why walk-forward validation still has the final say in this course.

points: An unconstrained decision tree is a high-variance model, close to the worst possible starting point for low signal-to-noise data like next-day price prediction

Bagging averages many trees trained on bootstrap resamples, cutting variance while leaving bias essentially unchanged, but correlation between trees, not tree count, sets the floor on how much it can help
Random forests add random feature subsets at each split specifically to lower that correlation, pushing the variance floor down further than plain bagging
For trading data, shallower trees, generous min_samples_leaf, and a reduced max_features fight overfitting more directly than adding more trees

Out-of-bag error is a genuinely useful, free sanity check, roughly 36.8% of rows are left out of any single tree, but overlapping triple-barrier windows can make it optimistic, so it should supplement, not replace, walk-forward validation
The next lesson contrasts this parallel, variance-reduction approach with gradient boosting's sequential, error-correcting one
